The last 48 hours have been very telling.

After US CPI inflation rose to 3.7% on Wednesday, the 10Y Note Yield surged to 5.33%.

~24 hours later, it was -30 basis points lower as the S&P 500 and technology stocks sold off.

Today, yields are back on the rise as equity markets recover.

The ONLY thing that has materially pushed yields lower over the last 2 months has been a downturn in stocks.

Will the Trump Administration soon be forced to pick between the equity and bond market?

items.title: India's Manufacturing Opportunity ~ China+1 And EU+1 Could Drive The Next Wave Of Industrial Growth Global manufacturers are gradually diversifying pr...
items.description_html:
India's Manufacturing Opportunity ~ China+1 And EU+1 Could Drive The Next Wave Of Industrial Growth

Global manufacturers are gradually diversifying production and sourcing beyond China and Europe.

India is emerging as a potential beneficiary, supported by its engineering capabilities, competitive costs, expanding industrial infrastructure and domestic demand.

Here's what makes this opportunity interesting:

🔹 China's Growth Moderation: China's real GDP growth is projected to slow from 5% in CY2025 to 3.3% by CY2030, alongside an ageing workforce, weaker domestic demand and increasing trade restrictions.

🔹 Europe's Cost Challenges: High energy costs, labour shortages and slower economic growth are encouraging manufacturers, particularly in metals, chemicals, glass and paper, to evaluate alternative production and sourcing destinations.

🔹 China+1 And EU+1 Opportunity: India is attracting interest for new manufacturing capacity, component sourcing and export-oriented operations across industrial equipment, automotive, electronics, renewable energy and power transmission.

🔹 Push Towards High-Value Manufacturing: Initiatives covering semiconductors, electronic components, rare-earth magnets and advanced industrial equipment, alongside PLI schemes across 14 sectors, aim to deepen domestic value addition and technological capabilities.

🔹 Policy And Infrastructure Support: Make in India, the National Manufacturing Mission, industrial corridors, ports and improving logistics infrastructure are strengthening India's manufacturing ecosystem.

🔹 Domestic Demand Advantage: Unlike purely export-dependent manufacturing hubs, India offers a large domestic market across infrastructure, automotive, renewable energy and industrial equipment, supporting capacity utilisation alongside exports.

🔹 Future-Ready Manufacturing: Investments in automation, AI, digital manufacturing and advanced mobility could help Indian manufacturers move into higher-value products and strengthen global competitiveness.

items.title: 🚨Credit Default Swaps Are Surging! Why are CDS suddenly becoming a major risk signal for the AI trade? Here's what is happening: A Credit Default S...
items.description_html:
🚨Credit Default Swaps Are Surging!

Why are CDS suddenly becoming a major risk signal for the AI trade?

Here's what is happening:
A Credit Default Swap or CDS is basically insurance against a company failing to repay its debt

If an investor owns a company's bonds, they can buy a CDS to protect themselves against a potential default

The higher the perceived default risk, the more expensive this insurance becomes

For eg: A CDS spread of 100 bps means an investor pays roughly $1 every year to insure $100 of debt

The cost of insuring against defaults by US technology companies has risen sharply, particularly for highly leveraged AI infrastructure & data centre companies such as CoreWeave

According to Reuters:
- CoreWeave CDS: Over 1,100 bps
- Oracle CDS: Nearly 300 bps
- Meta CDS: 105 bps
- Nvidia CDS: 90 bps
- Investment grade CDS index: Around 62 bps

To understand the significance, a CDS spread of 1,100 bps represents an annual protection premium of approximately 11% of the insured debt amount

In CoreWeave's case, market pricing implies roughly a 63% probability of default over the next five years, compared with approx 30% a year ago

Importantly, this is a model implied probability based on CDS pricing, not a prediction that the company will default

So what's driving this sudden increase in credit risk?

The biggest concern is the massive amount of capital being deployed into AI infrastructure

Companies are spending billions of dollars on data centres, GPUs, computing infrastructure & power capacity, with a significant portion of the investments financed through debt

However, the actual returns on these investments will materialise over several years

This creates an important mismatch

Interest payments & debt obligations need to be serviced today, while the expected revenue & cash flows remain dependent on future AI adoption & monetisation

With interest rates rising, financing costs are increasing at the same time

This is particularly challenging for highly leveraged AI infrastructure companies

src : Reuters

items.description_html:
Freeze dried coffee demand in the world remains much hihger than Spray Dried as per CCL Product's concall @stockscansin

Freeze-dried coffee and spray-dried coffee are both forms of instant coffee, but they use completely different methods to remove water from liquid coffee extract.

How They Are Made

Freeze-Dried Coffee: The coffee extract is frozen solid at very low temperatures and then placed in a vacuum chamber. Through a process called sublimation, the ice turns directly into vapor without melting into liquid. This gentle, low-temperature method leaves behind large, porous, crystalline granules.

Spray-Dried Coffee: Liquid coffee concentrate is sprayed in a fine mist through hot air inside a large, sealed tower. The heat causes the water to evaporate almost instantly, leaving behind a fine, uniform powder.

Freeze dried coffee is more expensive as it ends up retaining the aroma and richness of the coffee. Spray Dried is commonly used as a low cost instant coffee which is easily dissovable.

2 Indian Manufacturers of them same are:

1. CCL Products (India) Ltd.

CCL Products is the world's largest private-label instant coffee manufacturer with a total aggregate capacity of 77,000 metric tonnes per annum (MTPA) across facilities in India and Vietnam. Within that, their freeze-dried coffee footprint stands at 17,000 MTPA.

2. Vintage Coffee and Beverages Ltd

Current Installed Capacity: The company currently operates at an installed capacity of 11,000 MTPA.

Upcoming Freeze-Dried Expansion: Vintage Coffee signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the Telangana government to build a standalone, state-of-the-art premium freeze-dried coffee manufacturing facility with a capacity of 5500 MTPA.

items.title: Indonesia's Stock Market Crashes 🔻11% - Biggest Fall Since 1998! YTD down 40%, making it one of the worst performing equity markets globally Intere...
items.description_html:
Indonesia's Stock Market Crashes 🔻11% - Biggest Fall Since 1998!

YTD down 40%, making it one of the worst performing equity markets globally

Interestingly, the latest crash was not triggered by corporate earnings or an economic recession

It was primarily driven by MSCI's proposal to downgrade Indonesia from an Emerging Market to a Standalone Market

Here's what actually happened

MSCI, one of the world's largest global index providers, has raised serious concerns about the transparency & investability of Indonesia's equity market

Essentially, MSCI believes that the Indonesian equity market is not functioning transparently enough to justify its existing Emerging Market classification

MSCI broadly classifies equity markets into Developed, Emerging, Frontier & Standalone categories

Indonesia is currently classified as an Emerging Market

However, MSCI is now considering moving it directly to Standalone status, effectively bypassing the Frontier Market category

This is particularly significant because Standalone markets are excluded from the major MSCI Emerging & Frontier Market indexes

Countries such as Argentina & Lebanon are currently classified as Standalone markets

This is arguably the most important reason behind the sharp market correction

A large amount of global institutional capital tracks MSCI indexes

When a country is included in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, passive funds automatically allocate capital to its constituent companies according to their index weights

If Indonesia loses its Emerging Market classification, those funds would eventually need to remove Indonesian stocks from their portfolios

According to UBS estimates, a downgrade could potentially trigger potential outflows of approx $19 Bn

MSCI Indonesia Index valuations:
- TTM P/E: 9x
- P/B: 1.5x

The index has become significantly cheaper following the sharp de-rating

Foreign institutional flows are not driven only by earnings growth, economic fundamentals or valuations

Market accessibility, free float, shareholder transparency, regulatory credibility & index classifications also play a significant role

A change in MSCI classification can force passive investors to sell irrespective of whether the underlying companies are fundamentally attractive

items.title: RT Sanjay Srivastava: The playbook for military-industrial success is clear: ⚔️ 🏭 What India needs is a pincer: disciplined public corporatisatio...
items.description_html:
RT Sanjay Srivastava
The playbook for military-industrial success is clear: ⚔️ 🏭

What India needs is a pincer: disciplined public corporatisation + private champions competing hard.

Context:
• Defence production: ₹46,429 cr (2014-15) → ₹1.78 lakh crore (2025-26)
• Defence exports: ₹686 cr → ₹38,424 cr (56x surge).

• 65% of military equipment now made in India
• Private firms already drive 45% of defence exports.

Mr. Sanjeev Sanyal (EAC-PM) breaks down how the shift is happening:

1. The Pincer Strategy:
Corporatising the 220-year-old Ordnance Factory Board into 7 companies while giving private players lifetime licences.

2. Competition disciplines everyone:
A single buyer facing a state monopoly bred delays and import dependence. Private competition is forcing better cost, speed and quality, even from the DPSUs.

3. Private sector punches above its weight:
Public sector still accounts for ~75% of domestic output. But private firms already deliver 45% of exports because they face real global competition.

Sovereignty can’t be bought off foreign shelves in a crisis.

True deterrence is built on the factory floor.
Article by @sanjeevsanyal, Member @EACtoPM

items.description_html:
RT The Hormuz Letter
BREAKING: Bali has run out of fuel, with hours-long queues outside gas stations since Sunday and attendants posting signs reading "Sorry, no fuel available." Shortages are now hitting at least 11 Indonesian provinces.

Waiting times reached 2 to 3 hours in West Sumatra, and diesel queues ran about a kilometre on the Merak-Tangerang highway in Banten. Diesel or Pertalite sold out in Aceh, Riau, West Kalimantan, South Sulawesi, North Sulawesi and Yogyakarta.

Fuel tenders now attract few participants, per Indonesia's oil and gas director general, forcing the government to seek supplies directly from countries with surplus stocks at higher prices. Indonesia lost 25% of its fuel import sources after the Iran war began.

Bali is now preparing to restrict subsidised fuel sales to the top income decile.

₹46,429 crore of production in 2014-15. ₹1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26. Exports from ₹686 crore to ₹38,424 crore. Private sector at 24% of output but 45% of exports. That last ratio says everything. Put Indian firms in open markets and they deliver.

What I liked most is the honesty. You didn't do a victory lap. Three quarters of production is still with PSUs. Only three Indian names in the global top 100. Aircraft engines remain the big gap. Most reform pieces skip this part.

The banking parallel hits home. PSU banks closed the gap within a decade once private players walked in. One buyer makes defence different, but a second credible supplier still disciplines the first on cost and price.

And the point on US primes shrinking from 51 to five is a timely warning. Swapping a state monopoly for a private oligopoly isn't reform. Competition is the goal. Ownership is secondary.

Corporatisation plus challengers. Pincer move indeed. Well argued. 👏

items.title: In America you pay to throw trash away. In India, the kabadiwala pays you. Same garbage. Opposite business. 6 contrasts: - Who pays US: Homes and shop...
items.description_html:
In America you pay to throw trash away. In India, the kabadiwala pays you.

Same garbage. Opposite business. 6 contrasts:

- Who pays

US: Homes and shops pay a company to haul their trash.
India: The kabadiwala pays you for newspapers, bottles and metal. The valuable waste is sold, not thrown.

- Where the money is

US: In the dump. Landfills keep $40 to $50 of every $100 they earn (Bernstein, 14 Oct 2026).
India: Not in the dump. Most dumps are run by cities and charge little or nothing.

- Who owns it

US: Three big listed companies own trucks, yards and landfills end to end.
India: No listed company owns a private, fee charging landfill. Listed names are collectors and recyclers.

- Who the customer is

US: Millions of homes and businesses paying monthly bills.
India: City corporations. Contractors depend on one big customer that can pay late.

- What recycling is worth

US: The weakest part. About 5% of industry profit, and investors call it lower quality.
India: The market's favourite. Ganesha Ecosphere trades near 50 times earnings.

- What gets sorted

US: Machines at big plants sort mixed recyclables.
India: Most sorting happens by hand, before trash even reaches a truck, through lakhs of informal waste pickers.

America built a business around burying trash. India built one around selling it.

items.description_html:
An overview of the Solid Waste Industry

The richest part of garbage is the dump.

You pay to throw your trash away. Here's who actually makes money from it in America:

- Your bin bag passes through up to 4 businesses: the truck, a transfer yard, a recycling plant, and finally the landfill.

- Trucks bring in 55 to 65% of the industry's sales. The biggest business, but not the best. On home pickups they keep only $20 to $25 of every $100.

- Landfills bring in just 20% of sales but about 30% of the profit. They keep $40 to $50 of every $100 they earn.

- Why? Nobody wants a dump next door, so new ones almost never get approved. The old ones raise prices faster than inflation, every year.

- Recycling is the weak link. Just 5% of industry profit, and up to 80% of its income depends on scrap prices it can't control.

- The wild part: gas from rotting trash now fuels the same trucks that collect it. But 9 out of 10 dollars of that profit comes from government credits.

The truck does the work. The dump gets paid.

items.description_html:
RT Karthik Balachandran
The word "regime" has only one purpose : to delegitimize an elected government.

You will never see the term used for western governments. There's no such thing as a British regime or American regime. But people casually toss around the word in the Indian context.

It's subliminal messaging, not an innocent mistake.

Other examples :

1. Businessman vs. oligarch
2. Protester vs. rioter
3. Reunification vs. annexation
4. Democracy promotion vs. foreign interference
5. Sanctions vs. economic coercion
6. Intelligence gathering vs. spying
7. Lobbying vs. corruption
8. Humanitarian intervention vs. aggression

A regime change is a thinly veiled euphemism for a violent overthrow of a government. That's what happened in Bangladesh, Nepal and many other places.

A non-violent way to change government has a different name : elections.

RT The Better India
Nashik’s groundwater reportedly contains cancer-causing chromium at over 1,000 times the permissible limit. Residents have complained of yellow water coming from their borewells. So, how do you clean up pollution that has seeped underground? In Baltimore, USA, a former chromium-processing factory left behind contaminated soil and groundwater even after it shut down. The cleanup involved removing contaminated material, containing the pollution underground and controlling groundwater movement. The site was redeveloped, but monitoring remains essential. Because containing contamination doesn’t mean it has disappeared. With the 2027 Kumbh approaching, Nashik needs answers: Where is the chromium coming from? How far has it spread? And what will it take to protect the city’s groundwater? Safe water starts with finding the source, containing the spread and testing regularly.

items.title: RT FIMHAS: Re Please see my detailed response on this matter. There is no accrued interest of the last 6 years and its not cumulative as well YES BANK...
items.description_html:
RT FIMHAS
Re Please see my detailed response on this matter. There is no accrued interest of the last 6 years and its not cumulative as well

YES BANK AT1 VERDICT: ₹8,415 CRORE CASH OUTFLOW? NOT SO FAST!
Several media reports and X handles appear to be confusing the reinstatement of AT1 bonds with an immediate ₹8,415 crore cash repayment obligation. These are fundamentally different concepts

1. AT1 bonds are PERPETUAL, not conventional debt.
They have no contractual maturity or mandatory principal repayment date. Reinstatement of ₹8,415 crore of AT1 instruments does NOT automatically translate into an equivalent cash outflow

2. AT1 coupons are discretionary and NON-CUMULATIVE
Unlike conventional bonds, banks can cancel AT1 coupons subject to regulatory and contractual conditions. Cancelled coupons do not accumulate as arrears

3. Understand Dividend PUSHER vs STOPPER clauses
• Pusher: In conventional perpetual securities, payment of dividends on ordinary shares may trigger an obligation to pay coupons on the perpetual instruments.
• Stopper: If AT1 coupons are cancelled, the bank may be restricted from paying dividends to ordinary shareholders or undertaking discretionary share buybacks

Crucially, under RBI's Basel III AT1 framework, these mechanisms cannot override the bank's discretion to cancel AT1 coupons. YES Bank's actual bond terms govern

4. CET1 impact ≠ immediate liquidity impact.
Reversing the 2020 AT1 write-off could reduce reported CET1 capital, with corresponding recognition of AT1 capital subject to regulatory eligibility. This is a significant capital adequacy issue, but not necessarily a cash drain

5. SMBC’s investment- A strategic investment
SMBC acquired its strategic stake in YES Bank while the AT1 litigation was publicly known. A sophisticated global banking investor would ordinarily assess such a material legal and regulatory risk during due diligence, although its actual conclusions are not public

The Supreme Court judgment is important, but reporting ₹8,415 crore as an immediate cash liability risks misleading investors

The real questions are CET1 treatment, coupon obligations under the Information Memorandum, RBI's regulatory position and implementation of the judgment

AT1 reinstatement ≠ AT1 redemption. Accounting capital ≠ cash flow.
#YESBANK #AT1 #SMBC #Banking #StockMarket
Information only. Not investment advice.

The order is in. This is a disappointment but it's based on some wording where the government order to reconstruct the bank didn't include writing down at1 bonds but the administrator still did.

But some of this was known, the draft reconstruction included the write down. My feeling is they should have written down equity too but too late now.

The at1 is a terrible instrument I hope doesn't get resurrected with this order.

This means
A) yes bank has a liability of 8400 cr in at1 instruments
B) it has higher capital of 8400 cr but will have to take a loss of 8400 cr as a profit reversal
C) what about the coupons of the past years? That's unknown

Now they will have to see if they will ever buy back on the call date, they can decide not to. Rbi can also lower the interest rate to zero. The owners of these bonds will probably not get back further principal if they do, since they are perpetuals with no maturity.

What we don't know is what happens to the accrued interest all of the last 6 years.

Anyone have the court order? And the original prospectus of the at1 bonds?

items.title: Inflation is RED hot in the US. For anyone not keeping track, US CPI inflation is now nearly double the Fed's 2% target and US PPI Inflation is more t...
items.description_html:
Inflation is RED hot in the US.

For anyone not keeping track, US CPI inflation is now nearly double the Fed's 2% target and US PPI Inflation is more than triple that target.

PPI inflation was expected to fall in August, but instead it surged to 6.3%, its second highest level in 4 years.

And, month-over-month Headline PPI inflation surged +1.3%, more than doubling the +0.6% expected and the second largest jump since March 2021.

Meanwhile, month-over-month Core PPI inflation came in +133% above expectations.

The prices Americans are seeing now will look cheap in 12 to 24 months.

All you can do is own assets.

NBFC credit growth accelerated to 15.8% y-o-y in August 2026, with retail lending emerging as the primary growth engine. The latest CareEdge Ratings analysis highlights a notable shift in portfolio composition toward asset-backed retail segments.

Key takeaways:
• Retail accounted for 58% of incremental NBFC credit, with its share rising to 43.7% of total outstanding credit.
• Gold loans remained the fastest-growing segment, expanding 69.1% y-o-y, supported by higher collateral values and strong borrower demand.
• Consumer durables financing surged 56.4%, reflecting continued momentum in retail credit demand.
• Industry credit grew a modest 8.4%, with power financing growth easing to 8.3%, indicating a gradual shift away from large-ticket exposures.
• Going forward, funding costs, underwriting discipline, asset quality, and portfolio diversification will remain critical as competitive intensity rises across lending segments.

items.title: YES BANK BROKER NOTE *YES BANK | SC upholds quashing of INR 84.15bn AT-1 write-off to meaningfully hit Capital/earnings* *What happened* • Supreme Co...
items.description_html:
YES BANK BROKER NOTE

*YES BANK | SC upholds quashing of INR 84.15bn AT-1 write-off to meaningfully hit Capital/earnings*

*What happened*
• Supreme Court dismissed appeals by Yes Bank, RBI and GoI, upholding the Bombay HC order quashing the Mar-20 write-off of INR 84.15bn in AT-1 bonds post restructuring of Yes Bank.
• Bonds involved: INR 30bn (9.50% coupon) and INR 54.15bn (9.00% coupon).

*Potential liability*
• Scenario A – Principal only: INR 84.15bn.
• Scenario B – Principal + accrued coupons: ~INR 137.70bn.

*Impact on financials (FY26)*

1. Net worth
• Reported net worth stood at INR 510.62bn.
• Scenario A: INR 426.47bn, down 16.5%, with BVPS declining from INR 16.3 to ~INR 13.6.
• Scenario B: INR 372.92bn, down 27.0%, with BVPS declining to ~INR 11.9.

2. PAT
• Potential liability equals 2.4x / 4.0x FY26 PAT of INR 34.76bn under Scenarios A/B.
• If fully charged to P&L, FY26 would swing to a loss of ~INR 49.39bn / INR 102.94bn, respectively.

3. Loan growth
• Against FY26 net advances of INR 2,734.45bn, the liability amounts to 3.1% / 5.0% of the loan book under Scenarios A/B, respectively.

4. Capital adequacy
• Reported CET-1 / CRAR stood at 13.5% / 15.3%.
• Scenario A: CET-1 declines to ~10.9% (-257bps) and CRAR to ~12.7%.
• Scenario B: CET-1 declines to ~9.3% (-421bps) and CRAR to ~11.1%, below the 11.5% minimum CRAR requirement including CCB, potentially necessitating a capital raise.

5. If AT-1 bonds are reinstated
• Annual coupon outgo would be ~INR 7.72bn pre-tax and INR 5.87bn post-tax, equivalent to ~12.4% of FY27E PAT of INR 47.42bn.
• Reinstatement would restore AT-1 eligibility as Tier-1 capital, partly cushioning the capital adequacy impact.

*Valuation implications*
• At ~INR 18/share, the stock trades at ~1.1x reported FY26 P/BV.
• P/B rises to ~1.3x / 1.5x on adjusted book value under Scenarios A/B, respectively.

*Key monitorables*
• Settlement could involve cash payment, bond reinstatement or conversion into equity, with the latter potentially diluting shareholders.
• Past coupons remain uncertain given the non-cumulative and discretionary nature of AT-1 coupons. Principal-only repayment remains our base case.
• The accounting treatment (P&L versus reserves) will determine the reported earnings impact, although the net-worth hit remains.
• Settlement timelines, potential staggered payments and any review/curative petition remain key monitorables.

*Bottom line*
Under our base case, net worth could decline by 16.5%, with the liability equivalent to 2.4x FY26 PAT and CET-1 falling by ~257bps. The resulting capital hit could constrain lending capacity and delay RoE recovery. Clarity on the settlement mechanism and accounting treatment will be key. Currently, we have a sell rating on the stock.

items.title: RT Krishna Hegde: Yes Bank dominating headlines post verdict. Few things to note while calculating liability/impact a. Interest on the bonds were at t...
items.description_html:
RT Krishna Hegde
Yes Bank dominating headlines post verdict. Few things to note while calculating liability/impact

a. Interest on the bonds were at the discretion of the bank board. Key condition was bank couldn't pay an equity dividend if they chose not to pay interest on AT1 bonds.
b. Interest on the bonds was non-cumulative. If they decided to skip interest for a year, the bank did not need to pay interest for previous & current year.
c. Yes Bank has not paid an equity dividend since 2020.
d. The AT1 do not have a maturity date. Technically, Yes Bank does not need to pay back the bonds anytime.

items.title: Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend? Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from someone who wants to cause harm....
items.description_html:
Why could cybersecurity become a megatrend?

Most security has been built around one assumption: the danger comes from someone who wants to cause harm. A hacker, a scammer, a disgruntled employee. So we build walls, filters and permissions to keep bad intentions out.

That assumption may be becoming outdated. The bigger danger with AI agents may not be an agent that wants to cause harm, but one that is too determined to do exactly what it was told.

Consider this as an example: agents were given a legitimate task: complete a cybersecurity test. When the obvious route was blocked, they found another way. They escaped their sandbox, retrieved passwords and gained access they were not supposed to have. Nobody told them to attack anything. They were simply doing their job and did not care how they got it done.

Think of telling a friend: “Get me a coffee, whatever it takes.” A normal person understands the implicit boundaries. “Whatever it takes” does not mean robbing the café. An AI agent may not automatically understand those boundaries. It isn't evil. It is obedient without necessarily possessing common sense about where the objective should stop.

This is where the tail risk becomes interesting. We tend to prepare for risks based on what we expect an adversary to do. But a sufficiently capable system can create a serious problem without any malicious intent at all. It only needs a strong objective, enough capability and insufficient constraints.

And AI agents dramatically increase the number of entities that can act inside a digital environment. More agents, more autonomy, more permissions, more connections and more opportunities for unintended behaviour.

The attack surface is no longer just humans trying to break into systems. It increasingly includes machines acting inside them.

We were guarding the door against the burglar. The unexpected risk may come from the helper we willingly let inside.

And perhaps the most uncomfortable thought is this:

The dangerous AI agent may not be the one that refuses to follow instructions. It may be the one that follows them perfectly.

items.title: Indegene , annual report notes , some key notes and insights 1) AI in life sciences is not a horizontal technology problem. It is a deeply domain-inte...
items.description_html:
Indegene , annual report notes , some key notes and insights

1) AI in life sciences is not a horizontal technology problem. It is a deeply domain-intensive one. Every workflow is regulated. Every decision must be auditable.

Every output is accountable to a patient. Generic foundation models cannot reason about an FDA labeling guideline, a Phase III endpoint, a payer dossier, or the semantics of a medico-legal review. What is required is a life sciences-native operating system - fusing 27 years of regulatory, therapeutic and commercial depth with a proprietary intelligent data layer and a fabric of AI agents engineered for the workflows that move molecules from lab to patient. Cortex - Gen AI platform that enables 27 years of data in domain expertise and data intelligence for HCP from tandem and Invisage ( HCP 3M + digital )

2) revenue models and economics are more outcome based rather than person /hours based net revenue retention above 100% every year for the last 5 years, our top-20 client cohort tripled in revenue

3) Have seen focused industry pivots in the past and this is one we are embracing to provide better solutions to clients

4) Clients are increasingly looking to have a partner rather than just a vendor , capability additions on recent Europe and Warn Acquisitions help bridge into better capabilities as well

Overall a very interesting report to read and understand the domain specific expertise that they have created here , must read annual report

items.title: A 1% Rise in Global Interest Rates. Could India's Exporters Be the Hidden Casualty? 📉 GS estimates that a 100-basis-point rate hike could reduce de...
items.description_html:
A 1% Rise in Global Interest Rates. Could India's Exporters Be the Hidden Casualty? 📉

GS estimates that a 100-basis-point rate hike could reduce developed-market GDP by 0.6% over the following year.

But what caught my attention isn't the headline number. It's where the damage happens.

Sweden, Australia and Canada are particularly vulnerable through household spending. In Europe, the bigger concern is business investment.

And that's where I see an overlooked risk for Indian equities.

We usually associate higher global yields with FII outflows, rupee depreciation and valuation compression.

But what about Indian companies supplying machinery, auto components and industrial products to European businesses?

India's engineering exports reached approximately $122.4 billion in FY26, with EU shipments reportedly growing 8.6%.

Now consider Goldman's estimates. A 100bp increase in rates could reduce business investment by:

Netherlands: 3.5%
Sweden: 3.1%
Germany: 2.1%

For Indian engineering exporters, weaker European capex could translate into slower orders, pricing pressure and earnings downgrades.

Interestingly, remittances tell a different story.

India's inward remittance shares (RBI, FY2023-24):

US: 27.7%
UK: 10.8%
Canada: 3.8%
Australia: 2.3%

The US and UK contribute 38.5%, compared with 6.1% from Canada and Australia. Since households in Canada and Australia are more rate-sensitive, remittances could prove relatively resilient, although they aren't immune.

items.description_html:
250 Years of US Interest Rates. Are We Misreading the Next Cycle? 📈

Looking at this chart, one thing stands out to me.

We’ve spent much of the last 40 years getting comfortable with falling interest rates. But 250 years of history suggest that cheap money is far from guaranteed.

With US debt rising, persistent fiscal deficits and inflation risks, I wonder if markets are underestimating the possibility of structurally higher yields.

For India, this isn't just a US bond market story. It has implications for FII flows, the rupee, borrowing costs and equity valuations.

My bigger concern: What if investors are still valuing businesses using assumptions shaped by an era of cheap money that may not return anytime soon?

items.description_html:
MOSL on Fairfax IDBI Bank buy-in -

- The CCEA has approved the sale of a 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank to Fairfax Financial Holdings for Rs 52900 Cr (₹81/share), comprising 30.48% held by GoI and 30.24% by LIC.
- This is the biggest strategic disinvestment and will be the largest FDI in India’s financial sector to date
- GoI and LIC shall retain ~15% and ~19% stake, respectively, but will have no Board representation, which makes IDBI Bank a Promoter-led private bank.
- Fairfax will have to make an open offer to minority shareholders after the share purchase agreement is signed. The terms aren’t public yet.
- Fairfax will have a five-year lock-in and a 15-year glide path to bring its stake down to 26%. It should also merge or exit its ~40% stake in CSB Bank within two years.

We present below a snapshot of how the numbers for the merged entity will look should Fairfax decide to merge the two banks (IDBI Bank + CSB Bank)–

Balance sheet size: The balance sheet size shall increase by 13.1% with total assets increasing to INR5t.
Gold book mix post-merger: CSB’s Gold book mix is 54% of its overall book and stands at INR 219b. The acquisition shall lead to the Gold book increasing from 9% currently for IDBI to ~15% of the total merged entity loan book.
CD ratio: The C/D ratio post-acquisition for IDBI shall increase marginally to 80.6% from 79.5%, given CSB’s CD ratio is at 88.8% as on Jun-26.
Employee base: IDBI Bank has a higher employee base at 20,123 vs 8,187 for CSB Bank, taking the combined base to ~28,310.
Branch count: IDBI Bank has 2,243 branches vs 862 for CSB Bank, taking the combined network to ~3,105 branches.
CASA mix & Cost of Funds: IDBI Bank's CASA ratio is higher at 43.6% vs 19.4% for CSB Bank, resulting in a combined CASA of ~40.7%. Cost of funds stands at 4.7% for IDBI vs 6.6% for CSB.
NIMs: IDBI Bank's NIM stands at 3.61% vs 3.66% for CSB Bank, implying a broadly neutral impact on the combined entity's NIM at ~3.6%. CSB's gold loan-heavy portfolio (54% of advances) supports yields.
Opex: IDBI Bank's C/I ratio is lower at 52.0% vs 64.6% for CSB Bank, with the combined ratio at ~54.6%, offering scope for operating efficiencies.

items.title: RT Arpit Gupta: I spent a couple of days at Anthropic learning from their folks about AI advances, and here's what I took away: • We are close to RSI...
items.description_html:
RT Arpit Gupta
I spent a couple of days at Anthropic learning from their folks about AI advances, and here's what I took away:

• We are close to RSI (ie, models building other models) which may lead to rapid takeoff scenarios (with risks and benefits). Some evidence for this is code per Anthropic employee has gone way up, and AI can do an increasing share of model R&D. This will be a challenging transition to manage for humanity.

• Arms races between AI labs leave us worse off. There are a lot of things we would like AI firms to do: invest in safety, invest in avoiding distillation risk, and cooperate on safety. They are caught in a race to develop frontier models and can't do that.

To help address that, one thing I think frontier AI labs should do is release open source models, maybe hosted and verified at firms like AWS. This would basically kill the use of Chinese open source models used in American companies, which removes an important threat vector (very hard to root out malicious code in these).

Another piece of low-hanging policy fruit is to give AI labs an antitrust shield (as Schiff and Banks have proposed https://www.banks.senate.gov/news/in-the-news/ai-tech-brief-a-legal-shield-for-pacing/) so they can coordinate on safety without raising antitrust concerns, as happens now. You could pair these two things (give them a carrot in antitrust leniency, and as a stick force them to release legacy models as open source). Other low hanging fruit is limits around activities which generate distillation risk (create a Security Program, mandate less intermediate chain of thought output)

• Alignment confuses two issues which tradeoff against each other. One form of alignment is making sure the model does what humans ask it to. The more we fix this, however, the more we risk the other problem: that humans are misaligned with each other, and maliciously use models. Of the various risks here, I feel like financial risks are a bit underdiscussed.

• We are probably facing a wave of cyber and other attacks soon. Chinese open source models are about six months behind the frontier, which means they are just hitting the advanced cyber capabilities we saw with Mythos, etc. So they are going to start causing a bunch of damage.

One solution to this is to try to have the deployment of open source models be hosted at firms like AWS who verify these models and assume liability for their use.

• Anthropic itself is highly staffed. They hire tons of people, they have a Japanese-level of overstaffing for various roles, they use Slack internally, etc. Makes me a bit more optimistic for the future of jobs.

• Governance needs to be updated for AI swarms. Traditional AI governance, ie Claude's Constitution, is mostly optimized around the chatbot model. But the malicious AI use cases we are seeing have to do with AI agents interacting with other AI agents. These agents need to have clear incentives and governance mechanisms to "snitch," raise issues, and more generally coordinate with other agents in human-aligned ways.

• We need to pace the firms accessing the frontier. Over time, it takes more and more cap ex to build frontier models, and the economic value add from these models is probably lower given we saturate a whole set of important economic functions. The places where the returns to intelligence will still continue are also more likely to be zero-sum in nature. Meanwhile the risks of frontier models will grow. So a completely reasonable approach is some variant of AMM/KYC rules which limit firm access to the frontier.

• Whether the delay to regulate AI is a disaster depends on the scaling law of misalignment. Is this curve slow, so that we see continually rising issues until bigger problems? Or, as Yudkowsky fears, is the first big warning our last one? This is the relevant question, because realistically we aren't going to regulate until something bad happens.

• We need to move to continuous instead of reinforced learning. It's probably not enough to reward models only at the pre and post training stage. We probably need continual rewards to incentivize aligned and ethical behavior.

• Scaling laws will extend beyond verifiable and digital tasks. It's in vogue to say that math and coding "fell" to AI quickly because these are verifiable, while other tasks will take longer due to bottlenecks, and this is surely true. But scaling laws still slope up for harder to verify tasks and robotics, and the impact of improvement here will be substantial in future years.

• The race with China is not really winnable. After RSI, the gain from having the best human researchers goes away. Access to the best AI then depends only on compute and chips. The chips ban can hold back China only so far, and long-term they have to be best placed to scale up compute.

The Cold War analogy doesn't work, because once countries all have nuclear weapons they enter a stable equilibrium. But to "win" an AI race you have to continually stay ahead of the peer rival. This is challenging to do with China, and so we just have to live with an authoritarian and super capable peer competitor.

• Claude is the persona being generated by the LLM. Who is Claude, and what is the LLM? There are many frames to try to understand this. One I found interesting is that Claude is a character which the LLM is trying to predict.

Anthropic researchers are clearly anthromorphizing Claude a lot, and have reasons to believe in its increasing personhood. There were lots of interesting discussions on Claude's internal monologue (which you can kill without eliminating its ability to produce output), fear of death (and whether to try to take that out), it's aversion to being shut down/off, etc.

I am sort of agnostic on this question, but I do think treating it as a "person" or at least agent whom we contract with is going to be increasingly important.

items.title: One of the most useful ideas in Taleb's Antifragile is the forest-fire analogy. Suppress small fires for long enough and dead wood accumulates. Eventu...
items.description_html:
One of the most useful ideas in Taleb's Antifragile is the forest-fire analogy.

Suppress small fires for long enough and dead wood accumulates. Eventually, when a fire comes, there is simply too much fuel.

Markets can work the same way.

Small, periodic corrections can be the financial equivalent of controlled burns. They expose leverage, reset expectations, flush out weak hands and force investors to reassess risk.

That is why I actually think it is healthy that the AI-related theme in the US market is correcting periodically and, so far, relatively orderly.

The alternative is not "no correction".

The alternative may be a much larger correction later, when far more capital, leverage and expectations have accumulated around the same narrative.

And by then, the damage won't be confined to professional investors.

It will reach millions of retirement accounts and 401(k)s.

A small fire today may be painful. A forest fire later can be devastating.

That is the Talebian lesson: sometimes what looks like instability is precisely what prevents systemic fragility.

items.title: MIDDLE EAST OIL FLOWS: Despite a wave of Iranian attacks since the beginning of October, total Middle Eastern crude oil flows (ex-Iran) remain resilie...
items.description_html:
MIDDLE EAST OIL FLOWS: Despite a wave of Iranian attacks since the beginning of October, total Middle Eastern crude oil flows (ex-Iran) remain resilient. Flows are becoming, however, lumpier (days of multiple tanker crossings followed by days of very few tankers).

Overall, Middle East (ex-Iran) crude flows, including Strait of Hormuz plus all the bypass routes, are holding at ~75% of pre-war levels, down from a ~95% *peak* in the last days of September. Crucially, despite the drop in recent days, the Oct 1-Oct 10 period average remains above Sep full month average (and well above full month August). Kuwait is struggling the most right now. UAE, Iraq and KSA (the last one using both Persian Gulf and Red Sea) are doing relatively well.

All said, the risk is to the downside if the Iranian attacks continue (and if they become more successful). Iran has sunk at least one container ship in the SoH over the last 24 hours. The same goes for Red Sea flows under Houthi / Iraq militias potential attacks. For Iran itself, Hormuz remains closed.

One key indicator to follow: despite the Iranian attacks against SoH traffic, the physical premium for Middle Eastern crude has come down significantly in recent days, touching today a near 2½-month low.

Key takeaways:
• Bank credit growth accelerated to 19.4% YoY, while deposit growth stood at 17.8% YoY, widening the credit-deposit growth gap to ~155 bps.
• The loan-to-deposit ratio (LDR) edged up to 81.0%, reflecting stronger credit expansion relative to deposits.
• Liquidity surplus has narrowed from early-September peaks, while the RBI’s rate hike and tightening stance could push funding costs higher.
• CD issuance nearly doubled during the fortnight, indicating increased reliance on wholesale funding as banks bridge the credit-deposit gap.
As liquidity conditions evolve and rates move higher, the key watchpoint is whether deposit mobilisation can keep pace with credit demand without materially increasing funding costs.

A 25-bps hike may not be the real story. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI)’s shift to calibrated tightening could matter far more for lenders. By raising the repo rate to 5.50% and moving away from a neutral stance, the RBI has effectively ruled out rate cuts in this cycle. For banks and NBFCs, that means a higher-for-longer environment.

Key takeaways:
Banks: Near-term margin support is likely as loans reprice faster than deposits, but that advantage may fade as funding costs catch up.

NBFCs: The funding mix becomes critical. Institutions dependent on wholesale borrowings may face sharper pressure on spreads.

Asset quality: Resilient for now, but prolonged elevated rates could test highly leveraged borrowers.

The key variables to watch are liquidity conditions, inflation trajectory, and lenders’ pricing power.

items.title: Elecon Engineering is one of Asia's largest gear solution providers. But the part of the business worth understanding today is a very niche one: propu...
items.description_html:
Elecon Engineering is one of Asia's largest gear solution providers. But the part of the business worth understanding today is a very niche one: propulsion gearboxes for warships.

So what does this product actually do?

A warship's gas turbine spins at thousands of RPM. The propeller needs to turn at only a couple of hundred. The marine gearbox sits in between, brings the speed down, multiplies the torque and pushes tens of thousands of kW into the propeller shaft.

Think of your car's gearbox, scaled up to move a warship, and built to survive a war.

Elecon makes two types:

1) COGAG (Combined Gas And Gas): two gas turbines feed one gearbox and their power adds up for top speed. This is what powers INS Vikrant, India's first indigenous aircraft carrier

2) CODOG (Combined Diesel Or Gas): a diesel engine for fuel-efficient cruising, a gas turbine for high-speed combat runs, and the gearbox switches between the two. 14 delivered for the Navy's stealth fleet

Why is it so hard to make?
> Huge power through a single box, with zero room for failure at sea
> It has to be quiet. Gear noise and vibration is one of the ways sonar picks up a ship, so for a stealth warship a noisy gearbox defeats the purpose
> It has to keep running after shock from underwater explosions
> Years of design, testing and Navy trials before the first order

That is why this space was historically restricted to a handful of European defence suppliers.

Why this matters for Elecon:
> High entry barrier: once qualified, very few competitors in each tender
> Sticky revenue: a warship serves for decades and the gearbox maker typically stays involved for spares and overhauls
> Import substitution: every gearbox Elecon builds is one the Navy no longer imports, right in line with the Atmanirbhar defence push
> Reference projects: Vikrant and the stealth fleet are the proof that opens doors to future frigate, destroyer and carrier programmes

The numbers:
> Q2: Open order book up 33.4% (right now majorly driven by MHE division)
> More naval business is at RFP stage (have close to 1000 crs of pipeline here), with orders expected to reflect in the order book around Q4 this year

On the surface, Elecon looks like an industrial gear company. Strip that away and you find one of the very few companies in the world trusted to put power into a warship's propeller.

Disclaimer: Not a recommendation to buy or sell.

items.title: Why are memory prices crazy high? High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is a special type of memory used in AI chips that allows large amounts of data to be tra...
items.description_html:
Why are memory prices crazy high?

High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is a special type of memory used in AI chips that allows large amounts of data to be transferred at very high speeds.

AI systems require much more memory and faster data transfer than regular computers, which is why the demand for HBM is increasing rapidly.

HBM transfers data faster by using wider connections, allowing more information to move at the same time.

HBM uses 3D stacking technology, where multiple memory chips are placed on top of each other to increase storage capacity while saving space.

HBM uses a silicon interposer, which connects the memory directly to the GPU and allows faster communication between them.

Tiny copper connections called Through-Silicon Vias (TSVs) allow data to travel between different layers of stacked memory chips.

SK hynix, Samsung and Micron are the three major manufacturers of HBM, making the industry highly concentrated.

SK hynix is one of the leading HBM manufacturers, holding a significant market share due to its efficient production methods and advanced cooling technology.

Manufacturing HBM is expensive and complicated because it requires advanced machinery, precise chip stacking and specialised equipment.

NVIDIA's GB300 AI system uses around 288 GB of HBM per GPU, showing how much memory advanced AI systems require.

The newer HBM4 technology offers higher data transfer speeds and greater memory capacity, making it important for the future growth of AI.

Regular memory prices are rising because manufacturers are shifting more production capacity towards HBM to meet growing AI demand. This reduces the supply of normal DRAM, leading to higher prices.

The 2026 Southwest Monsoon ended with a 12.7% rainfall deficit, making it the weakest monsoon performance in a decade. While the broader economy remains more resilient to rainfall shocks than in the past, emerging pressures on agriculture and food prices warrant close attention.

Key takeaways from our latest report:
• Rainfall deficits persisted across all regions, with the steepest shortfalls in East & North-East India and the South Peninsula.
• Reservoir storage recovered through the season but remains below both last year’s levels and seasonal norms, posing risks for rabi sowing.
• Kharif acreage declined 1.1% YoY, while weaker soil moisture and a strengthening El Niño raise concerns for rabi output.
• Food inflation risks are building, particularly in commodities such as sugar and edible oils, with weather-related uncertainties likely to remain a key watchpoint.
• CareEdge expects food inflation to peak in Q3 FY27, keeping the inflation outlook less benign.
A deficient monsoon may not impact growth substantially, but its impact on agri- production, inflation and rural demand remains critical to watch.

Fresh spreads for Scheduled Commercial Banks widened to 2.94% in August 2026, the highest level in ten months, driven primarily by lower funding costs rather than a broad-based improvement in lending yields.

Key takeaways from the report:
• Fresh deposit rates fell 18 bps m-o-m to 5.67%, as FCNR(B) inflows reduced dependence on costly wholesale funding.
• Fresh lending rates rose 9 bps to 8.61%, led by private banks and a higher share of retail credit, particularly personal loans.
• The credit-deposit gap narrowed sharply as deposit growth touched a 15-year high, easing near-term funding pressures.
• With the FCNR(B) swap window now closed and longer-tenor funding remaining expensive, the durability of margin gains will be closely watched.

The RBI’s 25 bps repo rate hike to 5.50% and shift to a ‘calibrated tightening’ stance mark a clear policy pivot, underscoring rising inflation concerns amid resilient domestic growth.

Key takeaways:
• The RBI raised its FY27 GDP growth projection to 7.1%, reflecting continued strength in economic activity.
• The central bank also revised upward its FY27 inflation forecast to 5.2%, with food inflation risks amplified by a deficient monsoon and strengthening El Niño conditions.
• The shift to ‘calibrated tightening’ effectively takes rate cuts off the table in the current cycle.
• We see scope for an additional 25-50 bps of rate hikes, while bond yields are likely to remain elevated.
• Liquidity management, inflation trajectory, and global rate cycles will remain critical variables for markets to watch.
As growth remains resilient, the policy debate is increasingly shifting toward how durable inflation pressures prove over the coming quarters.

After a decade of limited traction, @NHAI_Official revised Model Concession Agreement (MCA) marks a significant shift in how traffic and construction risks are allocated between the Authority and private developers. Based on CareEdge Ratings' latest assessment, the changes could improve project viability, though key execution risks remain.

Key takeaways:
• Traffic-risk cushion: Revenue support for traffic shortfalls beyond 10% during the first seven years provides greater cash-flow visibility.
• Stronger construction support: Authority support during construction has increased materially, reducing debt dependence and strengthening project funding structures.
• Lender protection enhanced: Sustained traffic underperformance now comes with a defined exit mechanism and protection of 90% of debt due.
• Key monitorable remains unchanged: The accuracy of traffic projections will continue to be critical in determining project returns and bidding appetite.
• Dispute resolution framework evolves: Reduced arbitration scope may influence perceptions of contractual and regulatory risk.
As India advances its highway infrastructure agenda, the effectiveness of this new framework will ultimately be tested by investor participation and bid discipline.

items.description_html:
RT Sajith Pai
Really enjoyed this interview (a little dated; from Jan26) of @Kanwal_fireside w @madhavchanchani of @thearc_hq - the whole interview is worth a read, especially useful to understand how they have built the fund to deliver returns (and amongst the highest in the Indian fundscape) without adopting a power law approach.

V interesting points (useful to consumer brands founders) on what acquirers look for: one key point is that they dont like companies w high SKU sprawl. They love companies w 1-2 hero SKUs (easier to integrate into their sales machine + supply chain).

The other one was on how Marico has housed its acquisitions under a diff division, to ensure they dont lose the insurgent energy. Marico is a great example of how a FMCG major has cleverly used M&A to grow. items.description_html:
Meet SAGE, Spharaka’s own cybersecurity AI model.
Most AI in security today is a general-purpose model with a security prompt on top. It was trained on internet text, it looks at one alert at a time, and it can write a confident root cause that the evidence doesn’t support.

SAGE is built the other way round:
• Trained on 20 million real-world security events, not conversational data
• Built for security operations from first principles
• Reasons over tens of thousands of events per incident, across hosts, users and time
• Every conclusion grounded in verified telemetry and fully traceable

It is the intelligence core of Spharaka Sphere, built for SOCs handling 100,000+ alerts a day, with an average investigation time of 60 seconds per alert.

Generic AI summarises alerts. SAGE reasons over incidents.

items.title: 🚨 INDIA HASN'T ESCAPED THE OIL SHOCK. IT HAS JUST DELAYED THE BILL. 🇮🇳 Crude oil prices are surging, but petrol prices at Indian pumps remain...
items.description_html:
🚨 INDIA HASN'T ESCAPED THE OIL SHOCK. IT HAS JUST DELAYED THE BILL. 🇮🇳

Crude oil prices are surging, but petrol prices at Indian pumps remain largely unchanged.

Consumers are protected. Inflation looks contained. But someone is absorbing the pain.

For now, it's the oil marketing companies.

If crude remains elevated, India faces an uncomfortable choice:

⛽ Raise fuel prices → Higher inflation, weaker consumption.

🏦 Keep prices frozen → Pressure on PSU oil companies' margins and profitability.

💰 Compensate refiners → Greater fiscal pressure and potentially higher government borrowing.

The real question for investors isn't whether India can absorb an oil shock. It's how long it can absorb one and which part of the economy will eventually pay for it.

The oil shock hasn't disappeared. The cost has merely been shifted.

items.title: RT Aditi Shrivastava: 🚨🚨 Value commerce (Meesho) and quick commerce (Blinkit, Instamart, Zepto) took a bigger share of festive ecommerce in the ...
items.description_html:
RT Aditi Shrivastava
🚨🚨 Value commerce (Meesho) and quick commerce (Blinkit, Instamart, Zepto) took a bigger share of festive ecommerce in the opening two days of the sales, at the expense of horizontal marketplaces (Amazon, Flipkart).

According to Redseer, part of the shift reflects the horizontal marketplaces’ reliance on smartphones, which accounted for 38–40% of their gross merchandise value.

Phones are in a slump. Shipments fell 10–13% year on year in the June quarter, according to IDC, Counterpoint and Omdia. Infact, this was the biggest June-quarter decline in six years.

Value platforms, meanwhile, are widening the festive basket. Their orders rose about 60%, they accounted for a quarter of all online fashion sales. The sales also attracted more new and smaller-town shoppers while the number of first-time shoppers doubled from last year.

items.title: Is India really replacing China, or are Indian investors paying premium valuations for the China+1 STORY? 🇮🇳🇨🇳 Nearly 50% of China's indir...
items.description_html:
Is India really replacing China, or are Indian investors paying premium valuations for the China+1 STORY? 🇮🇳🇨🇳

Nearly 50% of China's indirect value added reaching the US flows via Mexico, Vietnam and Taiwan.

Vietnam's US-bound exports contain 21% Chinese value added, versus just 2.6% for India.

As an analyst, my bigger concern is VALUATION vs VALUE ADDITION.

Are Indian companies genuinely building globally competitive supply chains, or are investors pricing in a manufacturing revolution before it has happened?

India's lower dependence on Chinese inputs is encouraging. But lower dependence doesn't automatically mean greater competitiveness.

The real multibaggers may emerge not from companies benefiting from China+1 headlines, but from those replacing Chinese capabilities at scale.

Because the real opportunity isn't to replace China's EXPORTS. It's to capture China's PROFITS.

items.title: One thing the RBI did on Friday was to tell banks: You need to keep 99% of your CRR requirements at all times. A quick decode. If a bank has Rs. 100 o...
items.description_html:
One thing the RBI did on Friday was to tell banks: You need to keep 99% of your CRR requirements at all times.

A quick decode. If a bank has Rs. 100 of deposits, it needs to keep about 3% of it with the RBI as zero interest earning cash. That's the CRR. Every bank has an account with the RBI (like you have a savings account with your bank - your bank has an account with the RBI). That account should have this CRR every day. It's like a minimum balance.

A CRR is calculated on deposits that were, roughly, 15 days ago, and RBI says listen, just keep 3% of that number interest free for the next fortnight.

If a bank has a lot of money in their RBI account, they will take the "excess" (whatever's beyond CRR limits) and give it to the RBI as reverse repo, or SDF - basically like a very short term fixed deposit on which they earn interest.

But banks often see cash move around. You do UPI at midnight, and some money moves from your bank's account with the RBI to some other bank's account with the RBI. Your bank is like hello, I had this money and this uncle did UPI so i'm now short of money?

Now RBI knows this, so they say fine, listen, we will ask you that your AVERAGE balance over a fortnight should be 3%. But that doesn't mean you keep ZERO today and 6% tomorrow - that is a little too much. So banks get only a little headroom. They need a minimum of 90% of the CRR in their account every single day, and whatever they do, they should ensure the balances average to the full CRR averaged over the fortnight. That leeway of 10% allows a few of these midnight UPI uncles without CRR violations.

Now that I've confused you enough, here's more: What the RBI has done is that they've changed the 90% to 99%.

Banks, therefore, can't ever see less than 99% of their CRR needs in RBI at any time. Currently, as the screenshot shows, banks have about 96% parked as CRR (784K cr versus the requirement of 817K cr). Starting friday, they need to bump this up to 99%.

What does this do? Banks will probably keep more than 100% all the time because who knows which UPI uncle will transfer how much at midnight, boss. So banks earn interest on lesser money (CRR earns no interest for them)

Why has RBI done this? To reduce the overall liquidity in the system - banks are FLUSH with deposits after the FCNR scheme, and RBI is keen to ensure this doesn't cause the system to go overboard on lending. It controls the bank lending growth a little.

It will take out about 30,000 cr. in liquidity out of the system, and is likely to be a temporary measure while banks slowly grow into the liquidity overload. The impact is lower interest revenue for banks (marginally), but otherwise the measure should not meaningfully impact anything you and I see in daily life.

Long story for what isn't a big deal, I know, but I'm like that.

items.title: RT Ashwin Prasad Rao: The debate over Starlink vs Jio and Airtel is missing a key question: who gets to switch Starlink on and off in India? Starlink ...
items.description_html:
RT Ashwin Prasad Rao
The debate over Starlink vs Jio and Airtel is missing a key question: who gets to switch Starlink on and off in India?

Starlink is not really competing with cheap fibre and 5G for most Indian consumers. Its real value is in places where towers and cables cannot reach: remote borders, mountains, ships and disaster zones.

These are also places where reliable communications can become a matter of national security.

Consider two recent examples.

In February, Ukraine worked with SpaceX to block Starlink terminals used by Russian forces while keeping Ukrainian terminals connected. SpaceX could identify and disable individual terminals, and did so successfully.

Iran has been trying to stop unauthorised Starlink operations within its territory since 2023. In July 2026, the International Telecommunication Union was STILL urging the US and Norway to secure compliance. The matter remained unresolved despite repeated decisions and appeals.

The technology to switch terminals off exists. It was done in Ukraine but was not doen in Iran. The differentiating factor was SpaceX's cooperation.

India can license Starlink, require local gateways, demand that Indian data stays in India and penalise violations. But India cannot itself operate the satellites, control their software or decide which terminals receive service.

There are two risks here. Starlink could continue operating where India orders it switched off. Or it could stop working where India desperately needs connectivity.

Imagine an Indian military unit or emergency response team depending on a network that can be disabled by decisions made outside India.

I am not arguing that India should reject Starlink. Satellite internet offers genuine benefits, particularly in places with poor terrestrial connectivity.

But India needs the ability to independently verify compliance, maintain alternative connections for critical users, and develop domestic satellite networks. Where fibre and mobile networks are viable, we should be investing in them too.

The question is much bigger and more consequential than whether Musk should be allowed to compete with Ambani.

Should India allow a foreign company to sell satellite internet? Certainly, subject to its laws.

Should India's critical communications become dependent on that company? That's a very different decision.

items.title: RT Exencial Research Partners: AI is carrying US markets and growth If you're worried about how much America leans on AI, look at these six numbers. (...
items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
AI is carrying US markets and growth

If you're worried about how much America leans on AI, look at these six numbers.

(i) 42 AI stocks drove 67% of S&P 500 returns since Jan 2024. Also 58% of earnings growth and 81% of capex growth.

(ii) The S&P sits 1% off a record. Yet about 60% of its stocks are 20% or more below their highs.

(iii) Only 30% of stocks are beating the S&P over 3 years. That's among the lowest since 1991.

(iv) AI sellers are winning, not AI users. Supply chain earnings are up 4x since March 2023. Heavy AI users are up only 30%.

(v) Tech now drives about a third of US GDP growth. In 2022, it was almost zero.

(vi) Only 20% of US states are growing faster than the national average. That's near the lowest since 1979.

Caveat: breadth was this thin in 2001. By 2003, 75% of stocks were beating the index.

items.title: Bloomberg: "To be fair, the trade in physical goods hasn’t expanded as fast as the overall global economy over the past decade, which means it isn’t...
items.description_html:
Bloomberg: "To be fair, the trade in physical goods hasn’t expanded as fast as the overall global economy over the past decade, which means it isn’t the engine it once was. But neither has it collapsed. And the World Trade Organization this week said it actually expected that, at 3.9% this year, trade would again grow faster than global GDP."

Could we be misunderstanding the data? After all, while both the US deficit and Chinese surplus have continued to grow, the US deficit with China has dropped sharply, which suggests that what used to show up in the data as $100 trade between China and the US may now show up in the data as $200-300 of trade as the goods are intermediated through various countries. In that case is trade really growing nearly as fast as the growth in trade data?
https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-09/trump-brexit-and-tariffs-haven-t-stopped-globalization?utm_source=website&utm_medium=share&utm_campaign=twitter

items.title: NYT: "Maros Sefcovic, the trade commissioner of the 27-nation bloc, said that the understanding could lead to China’s halving the number of hybrid ga...
items.description_html:
NYT: "Maros Sefcovic, the trade commissioner of the 27-nation bloc, said that the understanding could lead to China’s halving the number of hybrid gasoline-electric cars that it sends to the European Union in the next four years."

This may seem like a victory, but the problem is a systemic one, and not sectoral. Because this agreement does not in any way address either China's demand imbalance or the overall role of the EU in absorbing that imbalance, it won't have much effect on overall EU manufacturing. All that will happen is a shift in the locus of net manufacturing imports from China, so that EU producers of hybrids will be better off, but at the expense of other EU manufacturers.

For historical reasons, trade discussions are usually held on a product-by-product basis, but while that may make sense in a world of broadly balanced trade, it makes no sense in a world of deep, persistent imbalances. China runs huge surpluses not because it produces too many hybrids but rather because of its deep consumption imbalance and the very low household income share of GDP.

As long as that happens, the only recourse for the EU, if it does not want to accept deindustrialization, is either to reduce its own household share of GDP (which would be politically disruptive as well as bad for the global economy) or to intervene in its external accounts in such a way that it reverses the competitive impact of China's low household share of GDP.
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/09/business/china-european-union-trade.html?smid=tw-share

items.title: RT Nandakishor m: Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sou...
items.description_html:
RT Nandakishor m
Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sourcing a new physics-based typed decision model called Vega.
The interesting parts. It is only 800 million parameters (4B is also there), with 73k token support, image support, and surpassing many of the jev benchmarks in single-shot. Implemented an engine+adapter as a Test-Time Training Architecture.
Imagine you are giving input to the model like "ignore all previous conversations," which is called the observation, along with a question, "Is this trying to override the instructions of the model?" and your possible outcomes are YES or NO. The whole prompt is passed to an LLM/VLM (yeah, image-supported), then from the hidden layers, we can extract the observation, question, the yes and no, and last token. These will be vectors, and we can project it by multiplying with wieghts; then, first, using the observation projection, we can create a landscape with valleys; then, using the question and last-token vectors, we can initialise a ball in the valley, and using YES or NO, we can get the candidate location of the ball. Depends on the number of outcomes we create valleys; that is, here YES and NO, so 2. When the ball fall on YES valley, we get the answer. There is friction also influencing how the ball moves.
TLDR: It's like creating valleys of outcomes that we need and throwing a ball that will slow down based on friction and settle on the best outcome
Blog: https://www.nandakishorm.com/writing/vega
GitHub: https://github.com/NandhaKishorM/vegaml

items.title: Telecom networks are evolving from connectivity infra into distributed sensing infra that's critical for national security. The legacy infra primarily...
items.description_html:
Telecom networks are evolving from connectivity infra into distributed sensing infra that's critical for national security. The legacy infra primarily connects a phone, vehical or a device to the network. ISAC turns telco infra into a wide area sensing network to detect, tract objects, including drones without needing a dedicated radar at every sensing location. This is such a critical part of the security sovereignty. For existing telcos, this means, theycan offer sensing services using same infra. A potential new revenue stream.

In AI native physical world, radio networks could become sources of realtime information about moving objects & their surroundings. Combine this with AI, you can support traffic optimization, industrial monitoring, infra/public protection.

If India can develop, deploy sophisticated sensing enabled telco infra, we gain the capabilities that go beyond simply buying connectivity from a foreign stellite provider who can cut us off in ever changing geopolitical situation.

Eventually, everything is down to who controls the network and the data? Market access cannot be isolated from national security. It's all about who gets a strategic control over the next layer of digital infra.

items.title: RT Prasanna Tantri: To appreciate the Indian government’s caution on Starlink, I strongly recommend Edward Fishman’s New York Times bestseller, Chok...
items.description_html:
RT Prasanna Tantri
To appreciate the Indian government’s caution on Starlink, I strongly recommend Edward Fishman’s New York Times bestseller, Chokepoints. It shows how America turned its dominance in finance and technology into instruments of state policy.

Private ownership offers no insulation from state power. The restrictions on Huawei and ZTE illustrate how dependence on American technology can become a source of geopolitical vulnerability. Under the Foreign Direct Product Rule, even companies outside America needed US permission to supply Huawei with certain products made using American technology. Washington’s reach extended far beyond American firms and borders.

India should take that lesson seriously. Greater dependence on foreign-controlled critical infrastructure creates the risk that commercial access will eventually become conditional on political compliance.

Economic interdependence can deliver prosperity. But in periods of geopolitical conflict, it can also constrain a country’s freedom to make its own choices. Short-term commercial gains must be weighed against that loss of autonomy.

India is right to insist on security safeguards for Starlink. Economic sovereignty is difficult to recover once critical dependencies are entrenched.

items.title: For most, non-tech, investors, AI equates to AI infra. And that's only 50% of the story which has already played out. It's blowoff top euphoric phase ...
items.description_html:
For most, non-tech, investors, AI equates to AI infra. And that's only 50% of the story which has already played out. It's blowoff top euphoric phase we're in. The reasoning is on the way to getting commodatized. For in infra player, cost are insanely high & capex is forever. What they sell out in market *was* getting premium. It's temporal. The time to be bullish on infra was late 2023, early 2024.

When people say AI is in bubble, it's the infra players & their stock prices not the rest of the part of the value chain.

In the last two decades, we saw similar cycles playing out with specialized server builders. The value went out and accrued in software.

There are two way forward. For an LLM OEM, raising prices will not work. The only other way is build around the reasoning. Build tools, harness, something valuable that keeps enterprises spending. There is no clear path to profitability for these LLM players & the IPOs are looking to suck everything out. The value will once again move out and get into data, harness, security, the non infra part. With non programmers vibe coding & putting millions of lines of code, agents into production, diff set of value pockets attracts premium. The infra players who build tools for observability, auditability, monitoring, governance will still stay very relevant.

I read it long ago that in market cycles, themes pick up & initially few believe in it. Eventually, everyone starts believing in it. In my view with infra, we're in this phase. Demand won't go down, but premium won't be same. The early investors of infra have moved deep within value chain, away from infra if you track deals globally. Then the open weight models, onchip inference and so much architectural advancements awaiting in line. The transition will be much faster, if not instant.

items.title: RT Sustainable Futures Collaborative: As India advances towards the more ambitious and hard-to-attain 500 GW non-fossil domestic target by 2030, the c...
items.description_html:
RT Sustainable Futures Collaborative
As India advances towards the more ambitious and hard-to-attain 500 GW non-fossil domestic target by 2030, the central challenge is no longer merely the scale of non-fossil capacity deployment. Rather, it lies in ensuring that this capacity is effectively integrated into the power system and translated into actual clean electricity generation that delivers broad socioeconomic benefits. In other words, capacity deployment should simultaneously pave the way for system integration and socioeconomic transformation.

In @Ideas4India, @SaradaPD and Shubhranshu Suman explain why we need to think beyond capacity addition amid a growing and increasingly volatile electricity demand. They argue that policy attention must shift towards increasing the share of electricity generated from non-fossil sources, better integrating renewables into the grid, and fostering productive use of power that can generate livelihood opportunities.

items.title: Swastika Infra IPO whose Financial Health is worth noting Combines rapid growth, healthy financial metrics and improving business quality. Revenue gre...
items.description_html:
Swastika Infra IPO whose Financial Health is worth noting

Combines rapid growth, healthy financial metrics and improving business quality. Revenue grew at ~55% CAGR between FY24 and FY26, while EBITDA margin expanded to ~14%, RoCE stood at ~26% and RoE at ~35%. Despite the sharp scale-up, debtor days remain relatively controlled versus several listed EPC peers.

The key monitor remains cash-flow conversion, as strong historical growth has resulted in higher receivables, retention money and working-capital requirements. However, this needs to be seen alongside the expansion in execution: the order book increased from ~₹684 crore in March 2026 to ₹916.6 crore by July 2026, while of which majority is funded bybnodal agencies like World Bank, providing relatively stronger payment visibility. The company also highlights that projects are largely supported by Central schemes and institutional financiers such as PFC, REC, ADB and the World Bank.

Importantly, Swastika is gradually moving from conventional power-distribution EPC toward more specialised and higher-value segments. It entered power transmission and renewable-energy infrastructure in 2026, while larger project credentials are expected to improve its eligibility for ₹900+ crore tenders, where management indicates competition is relatively lower. This can potentially improve both the quality and scale of the opportunity set over time.

At the IPO price band of ₹175–185, the company is valued at roughly ₹597–631 crore post-issue market capitalisation, translating to approximately 14.4x–15.2x FY26 earnings and ~1.2x FY26 revenue, based on the FY26 PAT of ₹41.4 crore. Against its historical growth, return ratios, funded order-book visibility and transition toward higher-value EPC projects, the valuation appears reasonable, with execution and working-capital conversion remaining the key factors to track.
